title: Ancient Civilizations Compared
description: Compare the major ancient civilizations of Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome, China, and India.
objectives: Identify common features across ancient civilizations
Analyze how geography shaped each civilization
Evaluate lasting contributions to the modern world

lessons.title: What Makes a Civilization?
lessons.content: Historians define a civilization by specific characteristics.
examples: Surplus agriculture → specialized labor → social hierarchy → government → writing → monumental architecture
River valley civilizations: all arose near major rivers for water, fertile soil, and transportation
Cultural diffusion: ideas spread between civilizations through trade and conquest

lessons.title: Legacy Comparison
lessons.content: Ancient civilizations left enduring marks on modern society.
examples: Greece: democracy, philosophy, Olympic Games, scientific method
Rome: law, engineering, Latin language, Christian church structure
China: paper, printing, compass, gunpowder, civil service examinations
Mesopotamia: first writing (cuneiform), first law code (Hammurabi)

title: Medieval World
description: Explore medieval Europe, the Islamic world, and East Asia from 500–1400 CE.
objectives: Describe feudalism and manorialism
Explain the significance of the Islamic Golden Age
Compare medieval Europe to contemporaneous civilizations

lessons.title: Medieval Europe
lessons.content: After Rome's fall, Europe fragmented into feudal kingdoms.
examples: Feudalism: king → lords → knights → serfs — land for military service
The Church unified European culture; Pope wielded enormous power
Crusades (1096–1291): Christian military campaigns to control Jerusalem; mixed results

title: The Renaissance and Reformation
description: Study the Renaissance and Protestant Reformation as transformative intellectual movements.
objectives: Explain Renaissance humanism
Describe the Protestant Reformation's causes and impact
Analyze how the printing press changed history

lessons.title: Renaissance Humanism
lessons.content: Humanism put human achievement and potential at the center, rather than theology.
examples: Civic humanism: being a good, engaged citizen is the highest virtue
Leonardo da Vinci: embodiment of the 'Renaissance man' — artist, scientist, engineer
Machiavelli's The Prince: analyzed political power realistically, not morally

lessons.title: The Reformation
lessons.content: Martin Luther's challenge to the Church split Christianity permanently.
examples: 95 Theses (1517): criticized indulgences — the Church selling forgiveness
Council of Trent (1545–63): Catholic Counter-Reformation cleaned up abuses
Religious wars devastated Europe for a century (Thirty Years' War 1618–48)

title: Atlantic World — Trade, Slavery, and Colonialism
description: Analyze the Atlantic economy built on colonialism and the slave trade.
objectives: Describe the Triangular Trade
Analyze the impact of the slave trade on Africa
Evaluate the long-term legacy of Atlantic colonialism

lessons.title: Triangular Trade
lessons.content: The Atlantic economy linked Europe, Africa, and the Americas in a brutal system.
examples: Europe → Africa: guns, textiles, manufactured goods
Africa → Americas: 12.5 million enslaved Africans (over 300 years)
Americas → Europe: sugar, tobacco, cotton, silver

lessons.title: Impact and Legacy
lessons.content: The Atlantic slave trade reshaped Africa and built European and American wealth.
examples: African states were destabilized; coastal kingdoms grew powerful through slave-trading
Enslavement built the wealth of Britain, France, the Netherlands, and the American colonies
Reparations debates today reflect the unresolved legacy of this history

title: Revolutions — American, French, Haitian
description: Compare the American, French, and Haitian Revolutions and their shared and different outcomes.
objectives: Identify Enlightenment ideas driving all three revolutions
Compare causes, processes, and outcomes
Evaluate which revolution was most radical

lessons.title: Enlightenment Foundations
lessons.content: All three revolutions drew on Enlightenment ideas about natural rights.
examples: Locke: natural rights (life, liberty, property); government by consent
Rousseau: the social contract; popular sovereignty
Voltaire: freedom of speech; separation of church and state

lessons.title: The Haitian Revolution (1791–1804)
lessons.content: The Haitian Revolution was the only successful slave revolt in history — creating the first Black republic.
examples: Haiti (Saint-Domingue) was France's most profitable colony; brutal enslaved conditions
Toussaint Louverture led enslaved people to defeat France, Britain, and Spain
Haiti declared independence Jan. 1, 1804 — forced to pay France reparations until 1947

title: Industrialization and Global Change
description: Examine industrialization's transformation of work, society, and global power.
objectives: Explain why industrialization began in Britain
Describe social impacts of industrialization
Analyze how industrialization drove imperialism

lessons.title: Industrial Revolution
lessons.content: Britain industrialized first due to a unique combination of factors.
examples: Coal and iron deposits, navigable rivers, strong navy, colonial markets, patent law protecting inventors
Enclosure movement: drove rural poor into cities as factory workers
Child labor: children as young as 5 worked 14-hour days in mines and mills

lessons.title: Industrialization and Imperialism
lessons.content: Industrial nations sought colonies for raw materials and markets.
examples: By 1914, European powers controlled 84% of the world's land surface
'Scramble for Africa' (1880–1914): Africa divided by European powers
Economic imperialism in China: opium wars forced China to accept British trade terms

title: WWI — Causes and Consequences
description: Examine the causes, course, and consequences of World War I.
objectives: Explain MAIN causes: Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism
Describe the experience of trench warfare
Evaluate the Treaty of Versailles and its consequences

lessons.title: MAIN Causes
lessons.content: WWI had deep structural causes underlying the assassination trigger.
examples: Militarism: European powers had built massive armies and navies for decades
Alliances: Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) vs. Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain)
Imperialism: competition for colonies created tensions
Nationalism: desire for self-determination; ethnic minorities in Austria-Hungary wanted independence

lessons.title: Treaty of Versailles
lessons.content: The peace settlement humiliated Germany and set the stage for WWII.
examples: War guilt clause: Germany solely blamed → $33 billion in reparations
Germany lost 13% of territory and all colonies
Redrew maps of Europe and Middle East creating new, often unstable nations
Hitler would later exploit German resentment of the treaty

title: WWII — Global Conflict
description: Study the causes, major theaters, and outcome of World War II.
objectives: Explain the rise of totalitarian regimes
Describe the Holocaust and its causes
Evaluate WWII's consequences for global order

lessons.title: Rise of Totalitarianism
lessons.content: WWI's aftermath produced totalitarian regimes in Europe and Asia.
examples: Hitler's rise: economic depression + German resentment + propaganda = Nazi takeover (1933)
Mussolini's fascist Italy (1922); Franco's Spain (1939); Stalin's Soviet Union
Japan's militarist government expanded aggressively into China and Southeast Asia

lessons.title: The Holocaust
lessons.content: The Holocaust was the systematic, state-sponsored murder of 6 million Jews and millions of others.
examples: 1933–1939: legal persecution, stripping of rights (Nuremberg Laws)
1941–1945: 'Final Solution' — systematic extermination via death camps
Auschwitz-Birkenau: largest camp; over 1 million killed
Nuremberg Trials (1945–46): established legal precedent for crimes against humanity

title: The Cold War
description: Examine the Cold War ideological conflict, major crises, and its global impact.
objectives: Explain the ideological divide between capitalism and communism
Analyze the Korean War, Cuban Missile Crisis, and Vietnam War
Describe how the Cold War ended

lessons.title: Cold War Crises
lessons.content: The Cold War nearly turned hot several times.
examples: Korean War (1950–53): first hot war of Cold War; divided Korea remains today
Cuban Missile Crisis (1962): closest the world came to nuclear war; Kennedy and Khrushchev's 13-day standoff
Vietnam War (1955–75): U.S. failed to prevent communist unification; 58,000 Americans and 3 million Vietnamese died

lessons.title: End of the Cold War
lessons.content: The Soviet Union collapsed due to economic failure, nationalism, and reform.
examples: Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika (1985): openness and economic reform
Fall of the Berlin Wall (November 9, 1989)
Soviet Union dissolved December 25, 1991 → 15 independent republics

title: The World Since 1991
description: Survey major world events from 1991 to the present.
objectives: Describe the post-Cold War world order
Analyze the September 11 attacks and the 'War on Terror'
Identify major global challenges today

lessons.title: Post-Cold War World
lessons.content: The U.S. emerged as the world's sole superpower — but the world remained complex.
examples: Globalization accelerated: trade, immigration, internet connected the world
Yugoslav Wars (1991–2001): ethnic conflict after communism; genocide in Bosnia and Kosovo
Rwandan Genocide (1994): 800,000 Tutsi killed in 100 days; world's failure to act

lessons.title: 21st Century Challenges
lessons.content: The 21st century brought new and ongoing challenges.
examples: 9/11 (2001): 2,977 killed; U.S. invaded Afghanistan and Iraq
Arab Spring (2010–12): pro-democracy uprisings across Middle East; mixed outcomes
Climate crisis: increasing urgency; Paris Agreement (2015) set targets
COVID-19 (2020): 7+ million deaths globally; exposed inequality in healthcare systems
